title: The Lemonade Stand
sum: On a hot Saturday, twins Maya and Leo turn Miss Dot's extra lemons into a lemonade stand to earn 100 cents for two ice pops.

cast.d: Leo's twin sister, seven, who likes to plan and count
cast.look: a seven-year-old girl with two puffs of curly dark hair, a yellow T-shirt and green shorts

cast.d: Maya's twin brother, seven, loud and quick to try things
cast.look: a seven-year-old boy with short curly dark hair, a red striped T-shirt and a gap in his front teeth

cast.d: the twins' calm dad, who is always reading a book
cast.look: a tall man with round glasses, a gray T-shirt and a paperback book

cast.d: the older neighbor next door with a big lemon tree
cast.look: an older woman with short white hair, a wide straw hat and a purple flowered dress
a medium-sized black-and-white dog with floppy ears

p: Saturday was the hottest day of summer. Maya ran outside in bare feet and hopped right back in. The porch steps were as hot as a frying pan!
Then a song floated over the rooftops, ding-a-ling, ding-a-ling. “The ice cream truck!” Leo yelled.
The twins ran for their piggy bank. Leo shook it hard. Something rattled! Maya pulled out the plug, and out fell one green button.
“That's not money,” Leo said. Outside, the song grew quieter and quieter until it was gone.
Dad looked up from his book. “The truck comes back at four o'clock,” he said. “Ice pops are 50 cents each.”
Two ice pops. One hundred cents. The twins had one green button. Leo flopped onto the cool kitchen floor. “It's too hot to earn money.”
Dad pointed out the window at the yellow lemons all over Miss Dot's grass. “Is it too hot for lemonade?” he asked. Maya and Leo sat straight up.
The twins raced next door. Miss Dot's lemon tree was so full that its branches bent over the fence. “Take all you want,” Miss Dot called. “It keeps making more.”
Maya held out the front of her T-shirt like a basket. Leo dropped in the lemons, one, two, three, four, five, six. Her shirt stretched almost to her knees.
“Roll them on the table first,” Miss Dot said. “Push down hard. Squishy lemons give more juice.”
Back home, the twins rolled every lemon under their palms until it felt soft. Then Dad cut all six lemons in half with a sharp knife.
Maya held up one half. Thin white lines split it into skinny wedges, and three flat seeds hid near the middle. “It's a bike wheel!”
Leo leaned in and sniffed it. “A sour bike wheel.”
They squeezed every half into a big pitcher. Juice ran down their arms and dripped off their elbows. Maya fished out the seeds, and Leo poured in cold water.
Leo took the first sip. His whole face scrunched up, from his chin to his eyebrows. He banged the table. “Sour, sour, sour!”
Maya laughed so hard she nearly fell off her chair. Then she tried it, and her face scrunched up too.
Dad slid the sugar jar across the table and went back to his book. The twins looked at the jar. Then they both grabbed a spoon.

art.s: In a sunny kitchen, a seven-year-old girl holds up a lemon half like a little wheel while her twin brother scrunches up his face after a sip from a big pitcher.

q.q: Draw one lemon half the way Maya saw it. What is inside?
look: a round shape like a wheel
skinny wedges split by thin white lines
three flat seeds near the middle
q.e: You looked closely, just like Maya!

q.q: Leo's whole face scrunched up. What does scrunched up mean?
q.e: Sour things make your face squeeze up tight, just like Leo's.

q.q: Dad cut six lemons in half. How many lemon halves were there?

p: Leo scooped sugar into the cold lemonade, one spoon, two spoons, three. The sugar sank like sand in a fish tank. Soon a little white pile sat at the bottom of the pitcher.
Maya grabbed a long spoon and stirred, clink, clink, clink. The white pile slid around, but it did not go away.
Leo took a sip. “Still sour!” Maya tried it next. Gritty! Tiny hard bits crunched between her teeth.
“Stir faster!” Leo grabbed the spoon and whipped it around like a mixer. Lemonade sloshed over the top and onto the floor. Pepper the dog trotted in, took one lick and sneezed.
Dad put down his book and filled two clear glasses. One got cold water from the fridge, and one got warm water from the tap. “One spoon of sugar in each, then ten stirs,” he said.
Maya stirred the warm glass, and by stir number five, the sugar was gone! Leo stirred the cold glass all the way to ten. A little white pile still sat at the bottom.
Maya held the warm glass up to the window. The water was clear. “Where did it go?” She took a sip. Sweet!
“It's still in there,” Dad said. “That's why it's sweet. Warm water breaks the sugar into bits too tiny to see.”
Leo looked at the white pile in the pitcher. “And cold water is really, really slow.”
Dad warmed a cup of water. Maya stirred in a whole cup of sugar, round and round, until the water turned clear. Leo poured it into the lemonade.
This time Leo took a big gulp, and his face did not scrunch up at all. He held out his cup for more.
Maya put four cups on a tray, one each for Leo, Dad, Miss Dot and herself. Leo dropped three ice cubes into each cup, plink, plink, plink. Then Maya filled them to the top.
They carried the tray next door. Miss Dot took a long sip and closed her eyes. “Now that,” she said, “is lemonade.”

art.s: At a kitchen table, twins stir sugar into two clear glasses of water while their dad watches and a black-and-white dog sneezes beside a puddle of lemonade.

q.q: Leo put three ice cubes in each of the four cups. Draw the tray. How many ice cubes in all?
look: three ice cubes in every cup
q.e: Three, six, nine, twelve. What a cold, yummy tray!

q.q: Maya could not see her sugar after five stirs. What was different about her water?
q.e: Her water was warm! Warm water breaks sugar into tiny bits fast. Cold water is slow.

q.q: Maya's lemonade was gritty. What does gritty mean?
q.e: Gritty means full of tiny hard bits, like the sugar that crunched in Maya's teeth.

p: Dad carried the old card table to the end of the driveway. Maya spread a blue towel over it. “We need a sign,” she said, “or nobody will know what we're selling.”
Leo grabbed a big sheet of paper and a fat red marker. He made a huge L, as tall as his hand. Then came E, then M, then O.
After the O, Leo ran out of paper. He squeezed the rest down the side in tiny letters. Maya tilted her head. “It says LEMO,” she said, “and then some ants.”
Maya took a new sheet. She spelled the word on her fingers, L-E-M-O-N-A-D-E, and counted eight letters.
She folded the paper in half, then in half again, then once more. When she opened it, the folds made eight boxes in a row. “One letter in each box,” she said.

Leo wrote the word again, one letter in each box. This time the last E fit just right. Under it, Maya wrote the price in big numbers: 25¢ A CUP. Leo set the cold pitcher on one corner so the sign would not blow away.
Leo tapped the price. “How many cups do we have to sell?” Maya counted by twenty-fives on her fingers. Twenty-five, fifty…
“The pitcher is leaking!” Leo yelled. Drops of water ran down the outside of the pitcher. A wet ring was spreading across the paper. The 25 had turned into a runny red blob.
Leo lifted the pitcher. There was no hole and no crack. He wiped it dry with his shirt, but new drops popped out all over it.
Dad came down the driveway with a roll of tape. “It's not leaking,” he said. “The air has water in it, too small to see. When that water touches something cold, it turns into drops.”
Maya thought for a second. “Like when I breathe on a cold window?”
“Just like that,” said Dad. He tore off four strips of tape, one for each corner.
When the paper dried, Maya wrote the price again, even bigger. They taped the sign to the front of the table. The pitcher went on a folded towel, far from the paper.
The twins ran to the stop sign and looked back. LEMONADE, 25¢ A CUP. They could read every letter from there. A man on a bike slowed down, read the sign and rang his bell.

art.s: At the end of a driveway, twins frown at a paper sign that says LEMONADE while drops of water run down a cold pitcher sitting on its corner.

q.q: One cup costs 25 cents. Maya counted 25, 50… Keep going. How many cups make 100 cents?
Draw the new sign for the lemonade stand. Make it easy to read from the stop sign.
look: LEMONADE with one letter in each box
big letters that all fit on the sign
q.e: What a sign! One big letter in each box makes it easy to read.

q.q: Why were there drops of water on the outside of the pitcher?
c: Water in the air turned into drops.
q.e: The pitcher was cold. Water hiding in the air turned into drops on it.

p: At one o'clock, the lemonade stand was open. It stood under the big maple tree, in cool shade. Pepper lay under the table with her chin on her paws.
Nobody came. A squirrel ran along the fence, and a car went by without slowing down. Leo drummed his fingers on the table.
At last Leo jumped up and cupped his hands around his mouth. “LEMONADE!” he shouted at the empty street. The squirrel shot straight up the tree.
Maya covered her ears. “Great,” she said. “You scared away our only customer.”
Then Sam the mail carrier came up the sidewalk, pink from the heat. Maya's mouth went dry. She knew what to say, but the words were stuck.
Leo poked her in the side. Maya took a big breath. “Would you like some cold lemonade? It's 25 cents.”
Sam wiped his forehead. “Yes, please!” He put three coins in Maya's hand: two small dimes and one big nickel.
Leo picked up the nickel. “This fat one must be worth the most.”
“Nope,” said Maya. “The little dime is ten cents. The big nickel is only five.”
Maya counted the coins twice and dropped them into the empty jar. Clink, clink, clink! Sam drank the whole cup in one long gulp, waved and walked on.
Soon a girl on a green scooter zipped up and paid with one shiny quarter. Slurp, slurp, gone!
By two o'clock, Maya's arms felt hot. She looked up. The table was not in the shade anymore. The shade had slid far over to the fence.
The ice cubes in the pitcher had shrunk to tiny chips. Leo took a sip and made a face. “It's getting warm,” he said, “and watery.”
And where was Pepper? She lay by the fence, right in the middle of the new shade. Maya squinted at the sun, then at the tree. “The sun moved across the sky,” she said. “So the shade moved too.”
Leo was already grabbing one end of the table. “Then we move too!” They carried it to Pepper's shade, step by step, while lemonade sloshed in the pitcher.
Dad came out with a bowl of fresh ice. Pepper opened one eye and closed it again.
At half past two, the gate next door squeaked. Miss Dot came over in her big straw hat. “One cold lemonade, please.” She dropped a quarter into the jar. Clink!

art.s: Twins carry a small table with a lemonade pitcher across a sunny lawn toward the shade of a maple tree, where their black-and-white dog is already lying by the fence.

q.q: Draw Maya asking Sam if he wants lemonade. Put her words in a speech bubble.
look: Maya and Sam at the stand
a speech bubble next to Maya
q.e: Maya's mouth went dry, but she said it! Your bubble shows her brave words.

q.q: At two o'clock, why was the table in the sun?
q.a: The sun moved across the sky, so the shade moved.
q.e: When the sun moves across the sky, shade moves too. Pepper found the new shade first!

q.q: Sam paid with two dimes and one nickel. How much money was that?
q.e: Ten, twenty, twenty-five. Just right for one cup!

p: At three o'clock, Maya peeked into the jar. Two dimes, one nickel and two quarters. She tapped each coin through the glass as she counted. “Ten, twenty, twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five.”
Leo tipped the pitcher and looked inside. There was only enough lemonade for one more cup. “One more customer,” he said, “and that's all we need.”
But nobody came, and the street was hot and still. At half past three, a lady with a stroller crossed to the other side. Leo lay flat on the grass and groaned.
Maya jumped up. She grabbed Leo's first sign, the one that said LEMO, and turned it over. On the back she wrote in big letters: LAST CUP! Leo held it over his head and hopped up and down.
Then they heard it, ding-a-ling, ding-a-ling. The ice cream truck came around the corner, right at four o'clock. It stopped in front of their stand.
Leo looked in the jar, and his shoulders drooped. “We're one cup short,” he whispered.
The driver climbed down from the truck. His shirt was damp, and his cheeks were red. He pointed at the sign. “Last cup? I've been in that hot truck all day.”
Maya poured the very last cup, right to the top. The driver drank it with a long sigh and dropped a quarter into the jar. Clink!
Back in the truck, the driver slid open his window. Leo held the jar up high. “Two ice pops, please!”
The man counted every coin and grinned. “That's just enough.” He handed down two ice pops, cherry red and covered in frost.
The sun was hot, and the ice pops started to drip right away. A red drop ran down Leo's wrist. Another one landed on Maya's toe.
“Eat fast!” Leo said. “It's turning back into juice!” They licked around and around the sides, drip, lick, drip. Pepper sat at their feet and watched every drop.
Maya crossed out LAST CUP. Under it she wrote two new words: SOLD OUT.
Miss Dot leaned over the fence and laughed at their red chins and sticky fingers. “Same time next Saturday?” she called.
Leo licked his stick clean. “Only if it's hot!”

art.s: In front of an ice cream truck on a hot street, twins lick dripping red ice pops beside a small lemonade stand with a SOLD OUT sign while a dog watches the drips.

q.q: Maya wrote SOLD OUT on the sign. What does SOLD OUT mean?
q.e: SOLD OUT means there is none left to sell. Every cup was gone!

q.q: The jar had 75 cents. The driver added a quarter, which is 25 cents. How much was in the jar then?
q.e: 75 and 25 make 100. Just enough for two ice pops!

q.q: Draw an ice pop in the hot sun. Show what the heat does to it.
look: red drops running down the ice pop
drops or a little puddle below it
q.e: Drip, drip! Heat turns a frozen ice pop back into juice.

fin.q: The twins paid for the ice pops with every coin in the jar. How many coins was that?
fin.e: Two dimes, one nickel and three quarters. Six coins made 100 cents!
First the lemons, then the sign, then the move to the shade, and last the ice pops!
